examples.ko: 가을철에는 일교차가 커서 감기에 걸리기 쉬워요.
examples.en: In autumn the temperature gap between day and night is big, so it's easy to catch a cold.
When autumn comes, the leaves change color on every mountain.

examples.ko: 가을철 별미로 밤과 고구마를 많이 먹어요.
examples.en: People eat a lot of chestnuts and sweet potatoes as autumn treats.
Autumn has nice weather, so it's good for traveling.

examples.ko: 가을철엔 낮과 밤의 온도 차이가 커요.
examples.en: In autumn, the temperature difference between day and night is large.
With autumn here, the number of hikers has jumped.

explain: '철'은 어떤 계절이나 시기를 말해서, '가을철'은 가을이라는 기간을 가리켜요. 하루를 말하는 '가을날'과 달리 건강이나 안전을 알리는 뉴스와 안내문에 자주 나와요. '봄철, 여름철, 겨울철'도 같은 식으로 써요.
explain_en: '철' refers to a season or period, so '가을철' points to the autumn period as a whole. Unlike '가을날', which means one day, it often appears in news and notices about health or safety. '봄철, 여름철, 겨울철' work the same way.

examples.en: Please don't touch my desk.
The child bumped the vase and it broke.
If you poke the sleeping cat, it will get angry.
My younger sibling keeps messing with my phone.
Who touched my bag?

examples.ko: 남의 물건을 건들고 가면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You shouldn't touch other people's things and leave.

explain: '건드리다'를 줄인 말이라서 대화에서 자주 들려요. 물건이나 몸을 살짝 만질 때도 쓰고, 상대를 일부러 자극하거나 시비를 걸 때도 써요.
explain_en: It is a shortened form of '건드리다' and is heard often in conversation. It can mean lightly touching things or the body, and also deliberately provoking someone.

examples.en: I scooped the soup with a ladle into a bowl.
The ladle fell into the pot and I am looking for it.
Buy a ladle with a long handle.
I stirred the stew using a ladle.
Please give me one more ladle.
The soup in the ladle was hot.

explain: 국이나 찌개를 뜰 때는 '국자', 밥을 뜰 때는 '주걱', 먹을 때는 '숟가락'을 써요. 모두 '뜨다'와 비슷하게 쓰지만 도구가 달라요.
explain_en: A '국자' is for scooping soup or stew, a '주걱' is for scooping rice, and a '숟가락' is for eating. They all go with a scooping action, but the tools are different.

examples.en: I turned the radio dial and made the sound louder.

examples.ko: 다이얼이 고장 나서 문이 안 열려요.
examples.en: The dial is broken, so the door will not open.
Old phones used a dial to enter the number.
Please turn the oven dial to the right.

examples.ko: 할아버지 집에는 다이얼 전화기가 아직 있어요.
examples.en: My grandfather's house still has a dial phone.

examples.ko: 작은 다이얼도 하나 있고 버튼도 두 개 있어요.
examples.en: There is one small dial and two buttons too.

explain: '다이얼을 돌리다'처럼 돌리는 동작과 같이 써요. 버튼은 누르고 다이얼은 돌려요. 전화를 걸 때는 보통 '전화를 걸다'라고 하고, 다이얼은 옛날 돌리는 전화기를 이야기할 때 나와요.
explain_en: It goes with the action of turning, as in '다이얼을 돌리다'. You press a '버튼' but you turn a 다이얼. To make a phone call people normally say '전화를 걸다', and 다이얼 comes up when talking about old rotary phones.

examples.ko: 식사가 끝나면 다 같이 뒷정리를 해요.
examples.en: After the meal, we all clean up together.
I'll do the party cleanup tomorrow.

examples.ko: 마지막까지 남은 사람이 뒷정리를 하고 가야 해요.
examples.en: The person who stays until the end has to tidy up before leaving.
Thank you so much for helping even with the cleanup.

examples.ko: 아이들이 놀고 난 뒤 뒷정리가 힘들어요.
examples.en: Tidying up after the kids have played is tough.

examples.ko: 캠핑이 끝나고 뒷정리에 한 시간이 걸렸어요.
examples.en: After camping, the cleanup took an hour.

explain: 일이나 행사가 끝난 뒤 어질러진 곳을 치우고 정돈하는 걸 말해요. 일 자체를 마무리하는 '뒤처리'와 달리 물건을 치우는 느낌이 강해요. '뒷정리를 하다'로 많이 말해요.
explain_en: It means tidying up the mess after a task or event is over. Unlike '뒤처리', which is about finishing off the matter itself, it mainly feels like putting things away. It is commonly used as '뒷정리를 하다'.

en: to think of something else; to daydream

examples.en: I was scolded by the teacher for daydreaming during class.
I was thinking about something else earlier, so I didn't hear the question.
When I'm tired, my mind keeps wandering.

examples.ko: 일할 때 딴생각하지 말고 집중해 주세요.
examples.en: Please don't let your mind wander and focus while you work.
If you start thinking about other things while studying, time flies.
I was lost in thought on the bus and missed my stop.

explain: '딴생각을 하다'를 줄인 말처럼 쓸 수 있어요. 시선이나 주의를 다른 곳에 두는 '한눈팔다'와 비슷하지만, '딴생각하다'는 머릿속으로 다른 생각을 하는 거예요. 보통 '딴생각하다가 ~했어요'처럼 실수 이유를 말할 때 자주 나와요.
explain_en: It works like a shortened form of '딴생각을 하다'. It is similar to '한눈팔다' (letting your attention go elsewhere), but '딴생각하다' is about thinking other things in your head. It often appears when explaining a mistake, as in '딴생각하다가 ~했어요'.

examples.en: When the rain stopped, the children ran out into the yard.
As soon as he took the call, he ran outside.
The doorbell rang, so I run out to the entrance.
When the door opened, the puppy dashed outside.

examples.ko: 할머니가 손자를 보고 신발도 안 신고 뛰어나가셨어요.
examples.en: Grandma saw her grandson and ran out without even putting on shoes.

examples.ko: 수업이 끝나자 학생들이 교실 밖으로 뛰어나갔어요.
examples.en: When class ended, the students ran out of the classroom.

explain: 밖으로 급하게 달려서 나가는 동작이에요. 말하는 사람 쪽으로 나올 때는 '뛰어나오다'를 써요. '뛰쳐나가다'는 더 급하고 격한 느낌이에요. 높임은 '뛰어나가셨어요'예요.
explain_en: It describes hurrying out by running. When someone comes out toward the speaker, use '뛰어나오다'. '뛰쳐나가다' feels more urgent and intense. The honorific form is '뛰어나가셨어요'.

examples.en: I stay away from sweet food for my health.
It is better to keep away from bad friends.
These days I am trying to stay away from my phone.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 사람들을 멀리하고 혼자 지내요.
examples.en: He keeps away from people and stays by himself.
I'm sorry that I kept my distance from my friend who had a cold.
Before an exam you have to stay away from games.

explain: '멀리하다'는 해롭거나 가까이하기 싫은 것을 일부러 피한다는 느낌이라서 사람·음식·습관에 써요. 반대말은 '가까이하다'예요. 단순히 거리가 먼 곳을 말할 때는 '멀다', '멀리 있다'를 써요.
explain_en: 멀리하다 carries the feeling of deliberately avoiding something harmful or unwanted, so it fits people, food, and habits. Its opposite is 가까이하다. For a place that is simply far away, use 멀다 or 멀리 있다.

examples.en: I got up at the crack of dawn and went to the airport.
My father goes to work at dawn every day.
I left at dawn, but the roads were still jammed.
It was exam day, so I went to school at dawn.
Today my eyes opened at the crack of dawn.

examples.ko: 새벽같이 시장에 가야 싱싱한 생선을 살 수 있어요.
examples.en: You have to go to the market at dawn to buy fresh fish.

explain: '새벽에'는 시간만 말하지만 '새벽같이'는 아주 일찍 서둘러 움직였다는 느낌이 들어요. '일어나다, 나가다, 오다, 출근하다'처럼 움직임을 나타내는 동사와 자주 써요. 같은 느낌으로 '아침 일찍'이라고도 하지만, '새벽같이'가 더 이르고 부지런한 느낌이에요.
explain_en: '새벽에' only gives the time, while '새벽같이' feels like you moved very early and in a hurry. It is often used with action verbs such as '일어나다', '나가다', '오다' and '출근하다'. '아침 일찍' is a similar expression, but '새벽같이' sounds earlier and more diligent.

examples.en: I joined a reading small group at work.
A small group has few people, so it's easy to talk.

examples.ko: 우리 동네 러닝 소모임이 매주 토요일에 모여요.
examples.en: The running group in our neighborhood meets every Saturday.

examples.ko: 소모임을 직접 만들고 싶은데 어떻게 하면 될까요?
examples.en: I want to start a small group myself; how should I do it?
This month's small group topic is movies.
My weekends are busy because of small group activities.

explain: 취미나 관심사가 같은 사람들이 모이는 작은 모임이에요. '동호회'는 조금 더 공식적이고 규모가 큰 느낌이고, '동아리'는 주로 학교에서 써요. 요즘은 앱에서 소모임을 찾는 사람도 많아요.
explain_en: It is a small gathering of people with a shared hobby or interest. '동호회' feels more formal and larger, and '동아리' is mostly used at school. Many people now find small groups through apps.

examples.ko: 날씨가 추워서 윗도리를 하나 더 입었어요.
examples.en: It was cold, so I put on another top.
I wore a white top and black pants.

examples.ko: 이 윗도리 사이즈가 저한테 좀 커요.
examples.en: This top is a bit big for me.
My top got wet, so I have to change.
This top has pockets, so it's convenient.
I bought the top and pants as a set.

explain: 바지나 치마와 짝으로 허리 위에 입는 옷을 말할 때 써요. 옷가게에서는 '상의'라는 말도 많이 해요. 편한 대화에서는 '윗도리'가 자연스러워요.
explain_en: It is used for clothes worn above the waist, paired with pants or skirts. In clothing stores you also hear '상의'. In casual conversation '윗도리' sounds natural.

examples.en: It rained a lot around this time last year too.
When this time of year comes, I think of my hometown.
Around this time, cherry blossoms start to bloom.
By this time next year, I want to be good at Korean.
Every year around this time I travel with my family.
The sky at this time of year is especially clear.

explain: '작년 이맘때', '내년 이맘때'처럼 해마다 돌아오는 같은 시기를 말할 때 써요. 지금 이 순간을 말할 때는 '지금'이나 '이때'를 써요.
explain_en: Use it for the same point in a recurring cycle, as in '작년 이맘때' and '내년 이맘때'. For this very moment, say '지금' or '이때'.

examples.en: Every night I write about my day in my diary.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 쓰던 일기장도 아직 서랍에 있어요.
examples.en: The diary I used as a child is still in the drawer too.
My diary is almost full already.

examples.ko: 제 일기장은 귀여운 고양이 그림이 있어요.
examples.en: My diary has a cute cat picture on it.
I want to start this year with a new diary.

examples.ko: 일기장 속에 오래된 사진이 한 장 들어 있어요.
examples.en: There is an old photo inside the diary.

explain: '일기'는 쓰는 글이고 '일기장'은 그 글을 적는 공책이에요. 그래서 '일기를 쓰다'와 '일기장에 쓰다'가 둘 다 자연스러워요.
explain_en: 일기 is the writing itself, and 일기장 is the notebook you write it in. That is why both 일기를 쓰다 and 일기장에 쓰다 sound natural.

en: live on one's own (cooking for oneself)

examples.en: I live on my own near the university.
It has been two years since I started living on my own.
When you live on your own, you end up cooking a lot.

examples.ko: 동생이 직장 때문에 서울에서 자취하고 있어요.
examples.en: My younger sibling lives on their own in Seoul because of work.
I went over to the house of a friend who lives alone.
When you live on your own, the monthly rent is the biggest burden.

explain: 비슷한 상황이라도 '하숙'은 주인이 밥을 해 주는 집에 사는 것이고, '기숙사'는 학교나 회사 건물에서 사는 것이라 자취와 달라요. 자취는 가족 집에서 나와 직접 집을 구해서 혼자 사는 경우에 써요. '자취방', '자취생'처럼 붙여서 말해요.
explain_en: In similar situations, 하숙 means living in a house where the owner cooks for you, and 기숙사 means living in a school or company building, so both differ from 자취. 자취 is for moving out of the family home and renting a place to live alone. It combines into words like 자취방 (rented room) and 자취생 (student living alone).

examples.en: I commute by subway.
I used to commute by bus.
From next month I will commute by bike.
My commuting time is too long.

examples.ko: 회사 근처로 이사해서 걸어서 출퇴근하고 있어요.
examples.en: I moved near my office, so I now commute on foot.
My home is close, so I don't get tired even when I commute.

explain: 가는 것은 '출근하다', 돌아오는 것은 '퇴근하다'이고, 둘을 합쳐 말할 때 '출퇴근하다'를 써요. '출퇴근 시간', '출퇴근길'처럼 다른 말과도 붙어요.
explain_en: Going to work is 출근하다 and leaving work is 퇴근하다, and 출퇴근하다 combines the two. It also joins other words, as in 출퇴근 시간 and 출퇴근길.

examples.en: Every evening I took a light walk along the lakeside.

examples.ko: 호숫가에 분위기 좋은 작은 카페가 있어요.
examples.en: There is a small café with a nice mood at the lakeside.
In the morning I saw a family of ducks at the lakeside.
I rested sitting on a bench at the lakeside.
On the weekend we pitched a tent at the lakeside and camped.
The lakeside breeze was cool, so I felt better.

explain: 받침이 없는 말 뒤에는 사이시옷이 들어가 '호숫가', '바닷가'가 되고, 받침이 있는 '강' 뒤에서는 '강가'로 그대로 써요. 물 가까운 곳은 이렇게 '물 이름 + 가'로 만들어요. [호수까]로 읽어요.
explain_en: After a word with no final consonant, a 사이시옷 (ㅅ) is added, giving '호숫가' and '바닷가'; after '강', which has a final consonant, it stays '강가'. Places near water are made this way: water name + 가. It is read [호수까].

examples.en: Before an exam, I breathe slowly and deeply.
The baby is breathing comfortably.

examples.ko: 산에서는 맑은 공기를 호흡할 수 있어요.
examples.en: In the mountains, you can breathe clean air.
You must not breathe through your nose underwater.
Do you remember how you breathed when you swam?
I learned how to breathe while exercising.

explain: 일상 대화에서 숨을 쉴 때는 '숨을 쉬다'가 자연스러워요. '호흡하다'는 운동, 수영, 의학, 명상처럼 숨 쉬는 방법이나 상태를 말할 때 써요.
explain_en: In everyday talk, '숨을 쉬다' is the natural phrase for breathing. '호흡하다' fits contexts about breathing technique or condition, such as exercise, swimming, medicine, and meditation.

examples.ko: 반 친구들이 모두 새 친구를 환영해요.
examples.en: All the classmates welcome the new friend.
We warmly welcomed the new employee.
We held a party to welcome the guests.
I want to welcome the newly arrived student.
Fans gathered at the airport to welcome the singer.
Thank you so much for welcoming me like this.

explain: 손님이나 새로 온 사람을 맞이할 때 써요. 행사나 가게에서는 '환영합니다'라고 인사하지만, 일상에서는 '어서 오세요'가 더 흔해요. 의견이나 계획에도 쓰는데 '그 계획을 환영해요'는 뉴스나 회의처럼 딱딱한 말투예요.
explain_en: Use it when you greet guests or newcomers. Events and shops say '환영합니다', but in daily life '어서 오세요' is more common. It also works for plans or opinions, but '그 계획을 환영해요' sounds stiff, like news or a meeting.
